Seven tones, one story

One invented course, Spreadsheets Without Fear, written seven ways. The facts never change. The order, the rhythm and the look do. Each tone below is the full landing page, live, then its post and the prompt to make one like it.

The course, Priya, Marta and every number are invented. The source facts.

  • VisionaryFor a reader who should feel that something new is possible.
  • StorytellerFor a reader who should see themselves in the problem.
  • EmotionalFor a reader who should feel something and remember it.
  • ExplainerFor a reader who should understand how it works.
  • Practical instructorFor a reader who should do it today.
  • AnalystFor a reader who should be convinced by evidence.
  • Executive briefFor a reader who should decide in three minutes.

Storyteller

Storyteller landing page, about 379 wordsOpen it full screen

The story order

Both follow the storyteller order: the hook (29 April, a shoebox, a bookkeeper's desk), the reader who wants something, the problem at three depths, the guide with empathy then proof, a three-step plan, one call to action, failure beside success, and an ending that returns to the shoebox; the course is not named before the fourth beat.

The facts check: every fact on the page and in the post, against the source.

The post: Facebook post, 287 words

"In my first year as a bookkeeper, a florist brought me a shoebox of receipts on 29 April, two days before her tax deadline. She cried at my desk."

Maybe you know that box. You run a small business. You are good at what you sell. You want to look at your own numbers and understand them. Instead, the receipts go in a box, or to someone else to sort, and the end of the month becomes something you dread.

Here is the part that matters: "She was not bad with money. Nobody had ever shown her a spreadsheet slowly."

The bookkeeper at that desk was Priya Shah. That shoebox is why she started Spreadsheets Without Fear. She has been a bookkeeper for 12 years. Since March 2025, four groups have taken the course: 71 people. 52 answered a survey afterwards. 44 said they now update their own numbers every week, and 39 said they had stopped sending their receipts to someone else to sort.

The plan is three steps:

  1. Register before 31 December 2026 for $199. After that, it is $249.
  2. Join six live Zoom lessons, Thursdays at 7pm Eastern, from 14 January 2027. At most 20 people per group.
  3. Build a cash-flow sheet, an invoice tracker and a price calculator with your own numbers, in Excel or Google Sheets.

Register on the course page: [needs: registration link]

If nothing changes, the box stays. If it does, here is how one past student puts it. Marta runs a two-person cleaning company: "I used to dread the end of the month. Now it takes me twenty minutes on a Sunday."

The florist had a shoebox and two days. You can start on 14 January.

The story order

Both run in the explainer's order: one question, the shoebox analogy, a worked example built from the course's real values, the same sheet stepped through column by column and row by row, a harder case (Priya's "not bad with money" story), questions to check yourself, and a recap that reuses the shoebox.

The facts check: every fact on the page and in the post, against the source.

The post: Blog article, 388 words

What would it take to keep your own numbers?

Think of a spreadsheet as a shoebox with dividers. Every receipt still goes in, but in a labelled slot. One thing per row. One kind of thing per column.

A worked example. Here is this course, written as a sheet.

   A            B
1  Lessons      6, weekly
2  Where        Live on Zoom
3  When         Thursdays, 7pm Eastern
4  Length       90 minutes each
5  Starts       Thursday 14 January 2027
6  Group size   At most 20 people

Now step it through. Column A says what a value is. Column B holds the value. Read across one row for one fact. Row 5: it starts Thursday 14 January 2027.

The course is "Spreadsheets Without Fear", for small business owners who avoid spreadsheets. You build three sheets with your own numbers:

  1. a cash-flow sheet
  2. an invoice tracker
  3. a price calculator

Excel or Google Sheets both work.

A harder case: what if you think you are bad with money? The teacher, Priya Shah, has been a bookkeeper for 12 years. Why she started it, in her words:

"In my first year as a bookkeeper, a florist brought me a shoebox of receipts on 29 April, two days before her tax deadline. She cried at my desk. She was not bad with money. Nobody had ever shown her a spreadsheet slowly."

Check yourself.

  • Which cell holds the group size? B6: at most 20 people.
  • What if you miss a lesson? Each recording stays available for 30 days.
  • What does it cost? $249, or $199 if you register before 31 December 2026.
  • Has it worked for anyone? Four groups, 71 people, since March 2025. 52 of the 71 answered a survey after the course. 44 of the 52 said they now update their own numbers every week. 39 of the 52 said they had stopped sending their receipts to someone else to sort.

Recap. A spreadsheet is a shoebox with dividers: one slot for each thing, so you can find it again. Six Thursdays, three sheets, your own numbers. Marta, a past student who runs a two-person cleaning company, in her words: "I used to dread the end of the month. Now it takes me twenty minutes on a Sunday."
